svg.text: FIGURE 4: SYSTEMATIC NODAL & MESH ANALYSIS AND SUPERNODE / SUPERMESH ARCHITECTURE
Equilibrium Matrix Formulations, Inspection Rules, Constraint Surface Equations & Computational Complexity

g.text: 1. Systematic Nodal Analysis Matrix
Equilibrium Matrix Formulation: [Y] [V] = [I]
• For network with n nodes, choose 1 Reference (Datum ∇ = 0 V).
• Number of Independent Node Equations: N = n - 1.
[Y_bus] · [V_node] = [I_inj]
• Applicable to planar AND non-planar networks equally!
• Node voltages are true single-valued scalar potentials relative to ground.
• Branch voltage: V_ab = V_a - V_b (positive at terminal a).
Inspection Rules for Passive Networks
Valid ONLY for circuits with independent current sources and resistors:
1. Diagonal Terms (Self-Admittance Y_ii > 0):
Y_ii = ∑ Conductances connected directly to node i
Always strictly positive; dominates the row (diagonally dominant).
2. Off-Diagonal Terms (Mutual Admittance Y_ij ≤ 0):
Y_ij = - ∑ Conductances connected between node i and j
Always negative (or zero if no direct branch exists).
Symmetry: Y_ij = Y_ji (Guaranteed for bilateral reciprocal networks).
3. Current Injection Vector I_i:
I_i = ∑ (Currents ENTERING node i) - ∑ (Currents LEAVING)
★ When Inspection Rules Break Down
• Inspection rules CANNOT be directly written if:
1. Dependent Sources are present: Destroys matrix symmetry (Y_ij ≠ Y_ji)!
2. Floating Voltage Sources are present: Zero branch resistance implies
admittance G = 1/0 → ∞ (Singular matrix!). Must use Supernode.
3. Mutual Inductive Coupling: Introduces non-diagonal coupling.
Remedy for Dependent Sources:
Express controlling variable in terms of node voltages, substitute into
nodal KCL equations, and bring coefficients to LHS into the [Y] matrix.
Result: [Y] matrix becomes non-symmetric, but fully solvable!
Cramer's Rule Formulation for Nodal Matrix
• For a 2-node system: [ [Y₁₁, Y₁₂], [Y₂₁, Y₂₂] ] · [V₁, V₂]^T = [I₁, I₂]^T
Δ = Y₁₁ Y₂₂ - Y₁₂ Y₂₁
V₁ = (I₁ Y₂₂ - I₂ Y₁₂) / Δ | V₂ = (Y₁₁ I₂ - Y₂₁ I₁) / Δ
• Driving-point input admittance at node 1: Y_in,1 = Δ / Δ₁₁.
• Transfer admittance between node 1 and 2: Y_21 = Δ / Δ₁₂.
• Always simplify resistors in parallel before assembling the matrix.
2. Supernode Analysis Architecture
The Supernode Physical Mechanism
• A Supernode is formed by enclosing a voltage source (independent or
dependent) connected between two non-reference nodes inside a boundary.
• Why needed? The current through an ideal voltage source is UNKNOWN
and CANNOT be expressed as (V_A - V_B)/R because R = 0 Ω!
• Solution: Treat both nodes plus the voltage source as ONE generalized node.
• Note: If voltage source is connected to Datum (Ground), NO supernode needed!
The non-reference node voltage is immediately known: V_node = ± V_s!
The Rigorous 2-Step Supernode Algorithm
Step 1: Generalized KCL on Supernode Surface
• Apply KCL to the closed Gaussian boundary enclosing nodes A and B:
∑ I_leaving(Node A) + ∑ I_leaving(Node B) = 0
• The unknown internal current through the voltage source cancels out completely!
Step 2: Constitutive Constraint Equation (KVL Inside)
• Write the internal potential relationship across the voltage source terminals:
V_pos - V_neg = V_source
• If source is dependent: V_pos - V_neg = μ v_x (or r_m i_x).
• Express controlling variable (v_x or i_x) in terms of node voltages.
• Combine Step 1 and Step 2 to obtain the exact required independent equations!
Exam Trap Drill: Dependent Supernode
Circuit: Node 1 connected to 20V source to ground. Node 2 and Node 3
connected by dependent voltage source 2 V_x with (+) at node 3.
Resistors: 2 Ω between node 1 and 2, 4 Ω from node 2 to ground, 8 Ω from node 3 to ground. V_x is across 2 Ω (V₁ - V₂).
Constraint Equation (Inside Supernode 2-3):
V₃ - V₂ = 2 V_x = 2 (V₁ - V₂) = 2 (20 - V₂) = 40 - 2 V₂
V₃ + V₂ = 40 ⇒ V₃ = 40 - V₂
Supernode KCL Equation:
Multiply by 8: 4(V₂ - 20) + 2 V₂ + V₃ = 0 ⇒ 6 V₂ - 80 + (40 - V₂) = 0 ⇒ 5 V₂ = 40 ⇒ V₂ = 8 V, V₃ = 32 V!
Supernode Properties & Dimension Counts
• If network has n nodes and k independent/dependent voltage sources:
KCL Equations Required = (n - 1) - k
Constraint Equations Required = k
Total Simultaneous Equations = n - 1
• Any resistor connected in parallel with the voltage source inside the supernode
is REDUNDANT for finding other node voltages (voltage is already fixed by source!).
★ However, it DOES consume internal power from the voltage source!
3. Systematic Mesh Analysis Matrix
Planar Restriction & Equilibrium Matrix
• FUNDAMENTAL RESTRICTION: Mesh analysis is strictly valid ONLY
for PLANAR networks! (Cannot define "window-pane" meshes on crossings!).
• For non-planar networks, general loop analysis or nodal analysis is REQUIRED.
• Number of Independent Meshes: M = b - n + 1 (Euler-Poincaré nullity).
[Z_mesh] · [I_mesh] = [V_source]
• Mesh currents I₁, I₂, ... are fictitious circulating loop currents.
Inspection Rules for Planar Passive Networks
Valid ONLY for circuits with clockwise mesh currents and voltage sources:
1. Diagonal Terms (Self-Impedance Z_ii > 0):
Z_ii = ∑ Resistances around the perimeter of mesh i
Always strictly positive; represents total resistance in loop i.
2. Off-Diagonal Terms (Mutual Impedance Z_ij ≤ 0):
Z_ij = - ∑ Resistances shared between mesh i and mesh j
Always negative when all mesh currents are chosen CLOCKWISE.
Symmetry: Z_ij = Z_ji (Valid for reciprocal networks without dependent sources).
3. Driving Source Voltage Vector V_i:
V_i = ∑ (Clockwise Voltage RISES) - ∑ (Clockwise Voltage DROPS)
★ When Mesh Inspection Rules Break Down
• Inspection rules CANNOT be directly written if:
1. Current Sources are present: Voltage across an ideal current source is
UNKNOWN! Cannot write KVL through that branch. Must use Supermesh.
2. Dependent Sources are present: Destroys matrix symmetry (Z_ij ≠ Z_ji).
3. Arbitrary Direction Selection: If some meshes are clockwise and others
counter-clockwise, mutual signs flip to positive (+Z_ij).
Remedy for Current Sources on Perimeter:
If an ideal current source is on the boundary of only ONE mesh, that
mesh current is TRIVIALLY FIXED: I_mesh = ± I_source! Reduces unknowns by 1.
Branch Currents from Mesh Currents
• Boundary Branch (Only belongs to mesh 1): i_branch = I₁.
• Shared Branch between Mesh 1 and Mesh 2:
i_downward = I₁ - I₂ | i_upward = I₂ - I₁
• Branch Power: P_branch = (I₁ - I₂)² · R_shared.
★ DANGER: P ≠ I₁² R - I₂² R! Never square currents separately!
• Mesh method is optimal when circuit contains many series current sources.
4. Supermesh Analysis & Decision Matrix
The Supermesh Physical Mechanism
• A Supermesh is created when a current source (independent or dependent)
is shared between two adjacent meshes.
• The voltage drop across the current source is unknown. To eliminate it,
temporarily OPEN-CIRCUIT the current source branch!
• The resulting enlarged combined loop formed by merging the two meshes is the Supermesh.
• Note: The mesh currents I₁ and I₂ STILL RETAIN their independent identity!
Do NOT combine mesh currents into a single current!
The Rigorous 2-Step Supermesh Algorithm
Step 1: Outer KVL Around Supermesh Perimeter
• Traverse the outer boundary of the combined supermesh in clockwise direction:
∑ V_drops(Mesh 1 perimeter) + ∑ V_drops(Mesh 2 perimeter) = 0
• Bypasses the shared current source branch completely.
Step 2: Constitutive Constraint Equation
• Relate the two mesh currents directly to the shared current source:
I_mesh(aligned) - I_mesh(opposing) = I_source
• If source is dependent: I_mesh(aligned) - I_mesh(opposing) = β i_x (or g_m v_x).
• Substitute controlling variable i_x / v_x in terms of mesh currents.
• Together, Step 1 and Step 2 provide the exact required independent equations!
MASTER DECISION MATRIX: Nodal vs. Mesh Analysis
When faced with a complex circuit in GATE, evaluate these 5 criteria:
Circuit Attribute
Prefer Nodal Analysis
Prefer Mesh Analysis
Number of Unknowns
Graph Topology
Non-Planar circuits (MANDATORY!)
Planar ONLY (Crossing invalid)
Source Distribution
Many voltage sources to ground
Many current sources on perimeter
Branch Connectivity
Parallel branches / Common bus
Series cascade loops
Required Variable
Node voltages, op-amp inputs
Branch currents, inductor currents
★ Golden Rule: If (n - 1) == (b - n + 1), check source types!
Voltage sources with a ground node favor Nodal (instant answers!).
Perimeter current sources favor Mesh (instant known mesh currents!).
★ The 3 Most Dangerous Supermesh Traps
1. Dropping the Shared Resistor: Resistors in series with the current source
are removed in KVL, but DO dissipate power! Do not forget them in power calculations!
2. Mesh Current Disappearance: In the supermesh KVL, use I₁ for mesh 1 resistors
and I₂ for mesh 2 resistors! Do NOT write a single combined current!
3. Sign of Constraint: Make sure aligned mesh is (+), opposing is (-)!
Check: Does the arrow point in direction of I_aligned? YES!
